newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan land prices almost stable -- minister.
newsitem.headline: Japan land prices almost stable -- minister.

text.p: Japan's land prices have almost stabilised after sustained falls, National Land Agency Minister Kosuke Ito said on Friday.

Ito said the pace of the fall in land prices has been on a declining trend and added: "Prices of residential land in major cities have almost stabilised, and commercial land prices have also calmed down greatly."
He said it was the first time that land prices have shown signs of stablising since the bursting of the "bubble economy" of inflated asset prices in the early 1990s.

A land agency official said, however, that while it was true that residential land prices in particular were stabilising, Ito's comments should not be taken to mean that residential land prices had bottomed out.
"They have not completely bottomed out. That is why we have not used the words 'bottoming out' in our assessment," the official said.

The official, announcing the agency's assessment of movements in Japan's land prices in the January-March quarter, said that residential land prices were "increasingly showing a trend toward flattening out".
He added that the pace of decline in Japanese commercial land prices was slowing.
He said that in large urban areas, residential prices were flattening out and the pace of decline in commercial land prices was slowing.

Asked whether such factors as the rise in the consumption tax and the possibility of higher interest rates were having an effect on the outlook for land prices, the official said that there were many factors to consider and which deserved careful attention. He added, however, that the trend in land prices was not expected to change greatly over the next few months.
Ito said effective use of land was a key point in ensuring a fully fledged economic recovery and said the ministry's present policy was aimed at this goal and no longer at containing land prices.
He said the ministry would be able to come up with a more definite assessment after looking at data for May and June.
